st.t: Automated evaluation: Stable scoring can preserve bad rubrics
st.an: CollabSkill accepts that rubric quality must be examined rather than inferred from scalable or consistent judging, and extends the cluster with a concrete reference-free rubric-generation method plus a manual criterion-level audit. Its reported precision and recall address rubric coverage and grounding, not whether final automated scores measure professional quality, so the contribution is useful but limited.
qs: While a more scalable approach is to use LLM-as-a-judge provided with fine-grained rubrics, many task sources do not come with rubrics or only cover correctness, and manual rubric construction remains expensive, motivating our reference-free approach where we employ an agent to generate rubrics automatically.

The generated rubrics achieve a recall of 82.1% against the official criteria (998 of 1,216 official rubric items are covered) and a precision of 92.2% (297 of 322 of our items are grounded in official criteria), with authors judging all 322 of the generated rubric items as important for evaluating task quality.

kp.k: Real-worker evaluation complements autonomous occupational benchmarks
kp.d: The authors introduce CollabSkill to evaluate human–agent collaboration rather than assume autonomous performance transfers to human augmentation. The study comprises 93 U.S.-based workers recruited through Upwork, 386 sessions, more than 1,500 prompts and 165 distinct executed tasks across 10 O*NET sectors. Participants averaged 9.6 years of occupational experience. Tasks came from GDPVal, APEX and APEX-Agents, with workers matched by occupational background and randomly paired with agents. Lawyers appear in the APEX-Agents task pool, but the paper reports cross-occupational findings rather than separate legal-sector results.
qs: We introduce CollabSkill, a framework for evaluating human-agent collaboration on real-world occupational tasks.
During the study period, 93 human workers participate in CollabSkill, contributing 386 sessions across 10 O*NET sectors.
APEX-Agents: (1) Financial Analysts; (2) Lawyers; (3) Management Analysts

kp.k: Bayesian ratings model human and agent contributions jointly
kp.d: CollabSkill models each deliverable score as the additive contribution of latent agent skill, latent human skill and observation noise. Shared participants working with different agents provide connections for estimating their respective contributions. Agents are ranked by posterior mean minus three posterior standard deviations, penalizing uncertainty. The authors acknowledge that the estimated score does not distinguish occupational task skill from collaboration skill; it is therefore not a pure measure of AI collaboration competence.
qs: rather than treating human variability as noise, Equation (1) explicitly allocates a latent skill component to each human participant.
A limitation of the current formulation is that the estimated CollabSkill score does not separately identify task skill and collaboration skill.

kp.k: Collaborative rankings differ from autonomous performance rankings
kp.d: The five-agent CollabSkill ranking is Claude Cowork 76.738, Claude Code 74.778, Codex 71.267, Manus 71.204 and Gemini CLI 69.555. Among terminal-based agents, Claude Code leads in collaboration, whereas Codex exceeds Claude Code in the paper's solo evaluation and cited autonomous leaderboards. Table 5 gives solo scores of 77.17 for Claude Code, 78.02 for Codex and 79.44 for Gemini CLI. The authors conclude that autonomous capability alone does not determine collaboration quality.
qs: Among the five agents evaluated, Claude Cowork achieves the highest estimated CollabSkill (µ − 3σ) as 76.738.
for agent developers, human-agent collaboration requires targeted evaluation and optimization, as autonomous capability alone does not determine collaboration quality;

kp.k: Interface design influences collaboration beyond underlying model capability
kp.d: Claude Cowork and Claude Code both use claude-sonnet-4.6, but Cowork's graphical interface produces the higher estimated collaboration rating. The authors interpret this comparison as isolating interface design and favoring graphical interfaces across work beyond software engineering. They supplied installation assistance and repeated the comparison among participants reporting agent familiarity of at least 4 on a seven-point scale (N = 81); Cowork remained ahead at 76.403 versus 74.349.
qs: Claude Cowork and Claude Code share the same underlying LLM, so their comparison isolates the effect of interface design.
this comparison controls for installation friction, as we provided detailed installation guides and assisted participants who got stuck at the installation stage

kp.k: Human augmentation succeeds unevenly across worker skill levels
kp.d: Human–agent teams were compared with the same terminal-based agents running autonomously under an AI-researcher-engineered system prompt. Workers in the highest estimated CollabSkill quartile achieved a 74% win rate against this baseline, compared with 27% for the lowest quartile. The finding supports conditional, rather than universal, benefits from human participation: collaborative outcomes depend on the worker's estimated skill.
qs: top- quartile workers (Q4) achieve a 74% win rate against the autonomous baseline, while bottom-quartile workers (Q1) win only 27% of the time.

kp.k: Interaction quality matters more than interaction volume
kp.d: The authors used gemini-3-pro to code all 386 session logs against 11 Anthropic AI Fluency Index behaviors. Total observed behaviors correlated with session score (Pearson r = 0.262, p < 1e − 4), while turn count did not (r = 0.046, p = 0.371). Six behaviors had significant positive associations: defining the audience, communicating tone and style, providing examples, setting interaction mode, clarifying goals and specifying format. These are reported associations, not demonstrated causal effects of training interventions.
qs: Six of the eleven behaviors were significantly correlated with higher session scores

Notably, the raw number of user turns was uncorrelated with session score (r = 0.046, p = 0.371), suggesting that more interaction does not inherently lead to better outcomes and the quality of the interaction matters more.

kp.k: Prior LLM familiarity correlates with collaboration skill
kp.d: For the 76 participants with paired surveys, Section 6.2 reports a positive association between self-reported LLM familiarity and estimated skill (Spearman ρ = 0.297, p = 0.010), alongside delegation comfort (ρ = 0.238, p = 0.041); remaining attitudinal measures were not significant. The introduction instead assigns p = 0.041 to the practical-experience correlation of ρ = 0.297, an internal reporting difference. Although the authors frame practical experience as a driver of skill, the reported evidence is correlational.
qs: self-reported LLM familiarity showed a significant positive correlation with collaboration skill (Spearman ρ = 0.297, p = 0.010).
Comfort with delegating work to an AI agent also correlated positively with skill (ρ = 0.238, p = 0.041).
In contrast, none of the remaining attitudinal measures reached significance.

kp.k: Experience changes capability beliefs more than autonomy preferences
kp.d: Paired surveys show increased trust (∆ = 0.58, p = 0.004) and delegation comfort (∆ = 0.45, p = 0.039). Perceived capability shifted toward greater agent autonomy on the Human Agency Scale (∆ = −0.50, p < 0.001), but desired autonomy did not change significantly (∆ = −0.16, p = 0.105). Lower-skilled participants increased trust by 1.03 points versus 0.16 for higher-skilled participants (p = 0.028), and shifted perceived autonomy by −0.89 versus −0.13 (p = 0.001). The authors distinguish beliefs about what agents can do from preferences about meaningful human involvement.
qs: Participants reported increased trust (∆ = 0.58, p = 0.004) and delegation comfort (∆ = 0.45, p = 0.039).
the preferred autonomy level did not change (∆ = −0.16, p = 0.105), suggesting preferences about human-AI work allocation are governed by factors beyond perceived capability.

kp.d: Gemini CLI generates task rubrics, and Gemini CLI and Claude Code independently grade submitted deliverables on a 0–100 scale, with their scores averaged. An author audit of 27 GDPVal tasks across nine sectors found 82.1% recall and 92.2% precision against official criteria. For 135 sampled task–deliverable pairs, scores using generated versus official rubrics correlated at r = 0.66 overall and r = 0.72 after three author-reviewed outliers were excluded. The authors acknowledge using LLM judges rather than human graders as a limitation.
qs: The generated rubrics achieve a recall of 82.1% against the official criteria (998 of 1,216 official rubric items are covered) and a precision of 92.2% (297 of 322 of our items are grounded in official criteria)

kp.k: Findings have sampling limits and employment-use restrictions
kp.d: The authors caution that recruitment through Upwork and restriction to U.S.-based workers introduce selection bias. Coverage of only 10 of 20 O*NET sectors and limited statistical power prevent fine-grained subgroup analysis or claims of full occupational representativeness. They characterize individual human scores strictly as proxies for AI literacy within the studied collaboration setting and explicitly warn against using them for employment screening or other consequential decisions.
qs: we cannot conduct fine-grained subgroup analyses due to limited statistical power, and our sample is not yet representative of the full occupational landscape.
We caution against using estimated human skill scores to screen or evaluate individual workers for employment or other consequential decisions.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shao and coauthors argue that effective workplace augmentation depends on collaboration-specific agent capabilities, interface design, and workers’ AI fluency—not simply autonomous model performance.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain occupational study, not a legal-services market forecast. The authors report that Claude Code leads the terminal-based agents in collaborative performance, reversing its ordering relative to Codex in autonomous evaluations, while Claude Cowork ranks first overall despite sharing Claude Code’s underlying model. They interpret the latter comparison as evidence for the importance of interface design beyond software engineering. Human contributions also vary: top-quartile workers achieve a 74% win rate against the same agent operating autonomously, compared with 27% for bottom-quartile workers. The authors associate stronger collaboration with practical LLM familiarity and specific interaction behaviors rather than the quantity of interaction or most self-reported attitudes. Hands-on collaboration increases perceived agent capability, trust, and delegation comfort, but does not significantly change desired autonomy. Their forward-looking recommendation is to develop agents specifically to augment workers and preserve meaningful human control; they offer no quantified prediction of legal employment displacement, pricing changes, or market restructuring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest principally on a multi-occupation worker study, automated deliverable scoring, Bayesian skill estimates, autonomous comparisons, interaction-log coding, and paired surveys.
pts.d: The study includes 93 US-based Upwork workers, 386 sessions, more than 1,500 prompts, and 165 distinct executed tasks across 10 O*NET sectors. Participants averaged 9.6 years of occupational experience; 76 completed paired surveys. Tasks were sourced from GDPVal, APEX, and APEX-Agents. Gemini CLI generated rubrics, and Gemini CLI and Claude Code scored deliverables. The authors report rubric recall of 82.1% and precision of 92.2% against official GDPVal criteria; score correlation with grading using official rubrics was 0.66 across 135 pairs, or 0.72 after excluding three author-identified outliers. Their additive Bayesian model estimates separate latent human and agent contributions. Reported CollabSkill scores are Cowork 76.738, Claude Code 74.778, Codex 71.267, Manus 71.204, and Gemini CLI 69.555. Cowork retained first place in 71.3% of 10,000 bootstrap resamples. In Section 6.2, LLM familiarity correlates with estimated human skill at Spearman rho = 0.297, p = 0.010, and delegation comfort at rho = 0.238, p = 0.041; the introduction instead gives p = 0.041 for practical LLM experience. These are reported associations, not an experimentally established causal effect of training. AI-fluency behavior counts correlate with session scores at r = 0.262, whereas turn counts do not show a significant association. Survey changes include trust +0.58, delegation comfort +0.45, perceived autonomy −0.50, and desired autonomy −0.16, with only the last not statistically significant. Broader claims about job loss, inequality, and existing augmentation usage are contextual claims supported by cited literature, rather than labor-market outcomes measured in this study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe the study’s 2026 task setting and tested agent versions; future augmentation benefits are aspirations without a specified delivery timeline.
pts.d: The supplied document is labeled arXiv v2, 25 July 2026, and a COLM 2026 paper. Comparisons use gpt-5.2-codex-medium, gemini-3-auto, claude-sonnet-4.6 for both Claude interfaces, and manus-1.6-lite. Workers were matched to tasks by occupational background and randomly paired with agents, with installation guidance and assistance. The autonomous baseline used terminal agents in headless mode with an AI-researcher-engineered system prompt. Survey changes were measured after a short series of tasks, not longitudinal workplace deployment. The authors qualify generalization because recruitment was limited to US-based Upwork workers, only half of O*NET sectors were covered, and sample size prevented fine-grained subgroup analysis. They acknowledge that automated scoring substitutes for human grading and that their latent score does not separately identify task expertise and collaboration skill. Benefits over automation are conditional on worker skill; they are not claimed uniformly for all workers or occupations.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify agent developers, employers, and professional workers as the principal stakeholders; lawyers are included in task sourcing but receive no separate reported findings.
pts.d: For developers, the implication is to optimize and benchmark collaborative behavior and accessible interfaces rather than rely only on autonomous leaderboards. For employers, the authors highlight worker AI familiarity and the possibility that effective teams can outperform autonomous agents. For workers, practical exposure can alter trust and capability beliefs while preferences for meaningful involvement persist. The task pool spans diverse occupations, including lawyers through APEX-Agents, but the paper does not isolate effects for lawyers, law firms, in-house legal departments, legal clients, or access to justice. The authors explicitly caution that estimated human collaboration scores are study-specific proxies for AI literacy and should not be used in consequential employment screening or evaluation.
